label: Inconsistent Feedback and the Missing User Model
properties_json: {"teacher": "human", "order": 1, "section": "sec:ch-human", "statement": "Human feedback is inconsistent: teachers make errors, lean towards one valence and follow different “training strategies”, and inconsistent feedback “can cause considerable delay in the learning process”.", "openQuestion": "Whether a learner can estimate its teacher's reliability, bias and strategy during the interaction, separating teacher error from recognition error, remains untested.", "text": "Human feedback is inconsistent: teachers make errors, lean towards one valence and follow different “training strategies”, and inconsistent feedback “can cause considerable delay in the learning process”. Modest error rates are enough to cancel what the teacher contributes: with a scripted oracle, Advise became equivalent to learning without feedback at an estimated consistency of 0.55, and TICS improved convergence only while the probability of an erroneous instruction stayed below 0.3. Teachers also differ and change. Valence is biased, but not always in the same direction, from 69.8% positive rewards in Sophie's Kitchen to 75% to 82% negative feedback with plain TAMER in a grid world; depending on the trainer, silence means punishment or approval, and participants reported switching strategy during training. Learners nevertheless fix these quantities in advance: Loftin et al. set the trainer error probability at 0.2 or 0.05, while the rates later estimated from their participants were 0.085 for volunteers and 0.034 for crowd workers, and Christiano et al. assumed a fixed 10% chance of a uniformly random answer. As Arzate Cruz and Igarashi note, “a formal model of users” for interactive RL “has not been proposed”. Whether a learner can estimate its teacher's reliability, bias and strategy during the interaction, separating teacher error from recognition error, remains untested.", "version": "Section IX v4"}

label: Cost of Human Feedback and User Fatigue
properties_json: {"teacher": "human", "order": 2, "section": "sec:ch-human", "statement": "Human feedback is expensive and it fades.", "openQuestion": "Whether any combination of label format, query rule and generalization brings a robot task within one non-expert's session remains untested.", "text": "Human feedback is expensive and it fades. Lee et al. describe human-in-the-loop RL as “challenging to scale since human feedback is very expensive”: Christiano et al. used 700 human queries on MuJoCo and 5,500 on Atari, whereas Hejna and Sadigh's expert answered 36 to 100 queries in about 22 to 60 minutes, and random query selection is sometimes competitive with active selection. Teachers “give copious feedback early in training but very sparsely thereafter”: most of Knox and Stone's 9 TAMER trainers had stopped giving feedback by the fifth game, and “user fatigue” is among the open challenges named by Arzate Cruz and Igarashi. Each label also says little. A preference carries at most one bit, in Celemin et al.'s corrective framework a correction gives only a sign, with a magnitude the user sets before learning, and feedback usually applies only to the states where it was given. Methods therefore stay small: Yu et al. ran human experiments only on 5\\times5 Grid Pac-Man, because a grid run already lasts about 1.5 hours. Whether any combination of label format, query rule and generalization brings a robot task within one non-expert's session remains untested.", "version": "Section IX v4"}

label: Interpretation of Human Feedback
properties_json: {"teacher": "human", "order": 3, "section": "sec:ch-human", "statement": "The same human signal admits “different interpretations”: as reward, as a label on the policy, or as advantage relative to the learner's current behavior.", "openQuestion": "Whether a learner can infer, for each teacher and during the interaction, which reading a signal carries remains untested.", "text": "The same human signal admits “different interpretations”: as reward, as a label on the policy, or as advantage relative to the learner's current behavior. Feedback is “policy-dependent”: with a scripted virtual dog, feedback on one state–action pair changed sign with the perceived trend, with a mean of 9.8 when the dog improved against −18.3 when it held steady. People also use the reward channel “for future-directed guidance”: in Sophie's Kitchen, 15 of 18 participants rewarded objects not yet used. Each fixed reading has its own failure. Read as discounted MDP reward, human evaluations create “positive circuits”, which 86.6% of trainers created in an episodic grid world, while the myopic alternative encodes a policy rather than a goal. Reactions read from faces or voices fare no better as reward: in EMPATHIC only the reward class of an event was predicted better than chance, while models of advantage overfit, and vocal energy correlated with advantage for only 3 of 14 teachers. Whether a learner can infer, for each teacher and during the interaction, which reading a signal carries remains untested.", "version": "Section IX v4"}

label: Delayed Feedback, Credit Assignment and Recognition Errors
properties_json: {"teacher": "human", "order": 4, "section": "sec:ch-human", "statement": "Before a human signal can teach, it must be recognized and attached to the behavior it judges.", "openQuestion": "Whether a learner can tell, online and at task speed, which event a signal refers to remains untested.", "text": "Before a human signal can teach, it must be recognized and attached to the behavior it judges. Human reward arrives late, so learners need “credit assignment to create labels from delayed reward signals”, yet the delay is handled with constants that do not transfer: COACH used a delay of 6 steps (0.198 s) on a TurtleBot, Deep TAMER fitted a Uniform[0.2, 4] s window on Bowling, and on the robot Nexi action lag credited reward to the wrong action until turns were lengthened to 2.5 s. Signals read from faces, voices or EEG add recognition errors, often of the wrong sign: agents trained on predicted facial feedback at 62% to 73% accuracy were only a little better than random feedback, and on the robot Haru “the recognition error of human feedback” set learning back for a time. Words and gestures must be grounded, so most systems reduce them to fixed vocabularies, such as 33 fixed sentences or two predefined gestures. Unprompted reactions are the hardest case: in EMPATHIC they ran from 2.8 s before to 3.6 s after an event, yet most studies elicit posed signals. Whether a learner can tell, online and at task speed, which event a signal refers to remains untested.", "version": "Section IX v4"}

label: Lack of Evaluation with Real Users

Simulated users are used because “human trials are expensive, time-consuming, suffer from issues with repeatability”, yet “simulated oracles do not behave like humans”. A scripted oracle supplied all feedback for Advise and most of PEBBLE's results, and when people do teach, they are often the authors. Samples are small: Bignold et al. compared 10 participants per condition, and 4 of Knierim et al.'s 14 sessions survived intact. Benchmarks are altered before use and the teacher's experience is seldom measured, so results can rarely be compared. The gap is widest on robots: Knox et al. described their Nexi work as only the second project to train a robot exclusively from human reward, and closed-loop studies with several people on hardware, such as Koert et al.'s 20 inexperienced users on a real arm, are exceptions.
